subject: assassin bug
title: This Bug Coats Its Legs in Sticky Resin Before It Hunts

scenes.text: This bug gets itself sticky on purpose before a hunt.
In Australia's Kimberley, an assassin bug scrapes resin off spinifex grass and smears it over its front legs.
Scientists wiped the resin off. Now nearly two in three flies they touched got away.
With resin, the bugs caught prey 26 percent more often.
That counts as tool use: it takes something from its surroundings and uses it to hunt.
Even newly hatched bugs, raised alone, coated themselves. They're born knowing.

description:
An assassin bug in Western Australia's Kimberley region makes itself sticky before it hunts.
The bug, a species of Gorareduvius, scrapes resin from the leaves of spinifex grass and spreads it over its body, especially the front legs. In tests reported in Biology Letters in 2023, bugs carrying resin were 26 percent more successful at catching flies and ants; once researchers wiped the resin off, 64 percent of the flies the bugs touched escaped. Because the bug manipulates something from its environment to do a job, it counts as tool use, and even newly hatched bugs kept alone did it.
Which animal has the smartest hunting trick? Comment below.
first_comment: The researchers cleaned the bugs with makeup remover pads to run the test. Which animal do you think has the smartest hunting trick?
